title: EG-GRPO: Evidence-Guided Step-level Credit Assignment for Deep Search Agents

paper.title: EG-GRPO: Evidence-Guided Step-level Credit Assignment for Deep Search Agents
paper.abstract: Abstract LLM-based search agents demonstrate strong capabilities in long-horizon information seeking and reasoning, typically trained via reinforcement learning. However, existing approaches predominantly rely on trajectory-level outcome rewards, providing limited supervision for complex search and reasoning processes. Although step-level credit assignment offers a promising solution, obtaining reliable and task-grounded supervision for open-ended search remains challenging. In this paper, we propose E vidence- G uided G roup R elative P olicy O ptimization ( EG-GRPO ), a framework that derives step-level supervision from the evidence annotations available in synthetic deep search data. EG-GRPO identifies the first supporting citation for each required evidence claim and uses the newly acquired evidence to construct step-level process rewards. By representing the accumulated evidence as an evolving knowledge state, EG-GRPO further performs state-conditioned relative advantage estimation and combines the resulting step-level signal with the standard trajectory-level outcome advantage. Experiments on five challenging deep search benchmarks show that EG-GRPO generally outperforms standard GRPO and existing reward-enhanced and step-level RL baselines across different model scales. These results demonstrate that task-grounded evidence annotations can provide effective process supervision for credit assignment in deep search RL.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: As the capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance, deep search agents have demonstrated immense potential in tackling knowledge-intensive tasks ( OpenAI, 2025 ; Xi et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2024 ) . Grounded in the ReAct paradigm, these agents iteratively gather evidence within noisy web environments by alternating between reasoning, tool utilization, and observation, ultimately providing well-supported answers ( Yao et al., 2023 ) . To further enhance their long-horizon information retrieval capabilities, Reinforcement Learning (RL) has emerged as the prevalent paradigm for training deep search agents. Existing work typically uses a binary outcome reward as the training signal on synthetic multi‑hop QA datasets, comparing the agent’s final answer against the ground truth ( Jin et al., 2025 ; Gao et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025b ) . In deep search scenarios, a complete trajectory typically comprises anywhere from several to over a dozen retrieval iterations, with each retrieval action potentially exerting a critical impact on the final answer formulation. However, the entire trajectory receives only a single binary scalar signal at its conclusion, leaving the model unable to discern which specific retrieval step played the decisive role ( Shao et al., 2025 ) . To alleviate this reward sparsity issue, several studies have attempted to introduce richer reward signals at the trajectory level ( Gunjal et al., 2026 ; Lu et al., 2025 ) . E-GRPO ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) leverages entity annotations in synthetic data to formulate an entity matching rate as a fine-grained reward; CaRR ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) further decomposes questions into single-hop rubrics, combining context-aware rubric rewards and outcome rewards in RL. Although these methods yield substantial improvements in their respective evaluation settings, they fundamentally still calculate a scalar reward for the entire trajectory. Consequently, the core issue of differentiated step-level credit assignment remains unresolved. Step-level credit assignment provides a more direct approach to alleviating the aforementioned problem and has been extensively studied in sequential reasoning ( Zhang, 2026 ; Guo et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . Process Reward Models (PRMs) provide step-level supervision over intermediate reasoning steps, offering a more direct training signal than outcome-only rewards ( Lightman et al., 2024 ; Pala et al., 2025 ) . Meanwhile, GiGPO ( Feng et al., 2025 ) introduces state-based grouping to estimate step-level relative advantages for long-horizon LLM agents. Recently, STAMP ( Xu et al., 2026 ) further extends step-level credit assignment to deep search agents by tracing evidence provenance and attributing credit to the first retrieval action that exposes supporting evidence. However, applying such approaches to open-ended deep search still faces two key challenges. First, search actions lack a well-defined notion of local correctness: a retrieval step may be valuable for discovering direct evidence, uncovering indirect clues, or narrowing the search space, making reliable and task-grounded step-level supervision difficult to obtain. Second, fine-grained credit assignment requires a meaningful representation of the evolving search state, whereas raw multi-turn search histories are highly heterogeneous and difficult to match reliably. These challenges motivate us to look beyond external process supervision and ask whether a task-grounded step-level signal is already available in the synthetic data used to train deep search agents. Figure 1: Left: Distribution of overall evidence coverage across correct and incorrect trajectories, showing that task success strongly correlates with higher coverage. Right: Trajectory-wise cumulative evidence coverage over normalized search progress, demonstrating that correct trajectories consistently accumulate evidence faster from the early search stages. We observe that such supervisory signals are inherently embedded in synthetic data pipelines. Current deep search datasets are often constructed through knowledge‑graph random walks and information obfuscation, which produce structured annotations describing the factual evidence needed to answer each query ( Lu et al., 2025 ; Du et al., 2026 ) . Traditionally, only question‑answer pairs are retained for reward computation, discarding this rich annotation. However, the annotated evidence claims provide a natural source of task-grounded step-level supervision, as they specify the factual information that a successful trajectory should progressively acquire. To test this hypothesis, we conducted an experiment on a subset of the training set (320 prompts) by sampling 8 trajectories per prompt and computing the evidence coverage rate for each trajectory. Figure 1 (left) shows that correct trajectories have significantly higher coverage (median 41.97% vs. 26.29%), confirming coverage as a strong predictor of final correctness. Figure 1 (right) further reveals that correct trajectories maintain higher cumulative coverage from the very beginning, and this gap widens as retrieval proceeds. These observations indicate that evidence acquisition is a continuous process signal highly correlated with task success. More importantly, the cumulative set of acquired evidence claims provides an explicit representation of the agent’s evolving knowledge state, allowing rollouts to be compared under identical evidence states without manual process annotation. This observation motivates us to use task-grounded evidence annotations as a source of step-level supervision for deep search RL. Building upon these insights, we propose E vidence- G uided G roup R elative P olicy O ptimization ( EG-GRPO ), a step-level credit assignment method for deep search agents. EG-GRPO transforms the evidence claims annotated in synthetic data into dense process rewards and combines them with GRPO’s trajectory-level advantages, preserving outcome supervision while providing fine-grained guidance for intermediate retrieval actions. Specifically, an LLM-based judge identifies the first supporting citation for each required evidence claim, and newly supported claims at each step are converted into process rewards. We further define a cumulative knowledge state based on the evidence claims acquired before each step and perform state-conditioned advantage normalization, enabling different rollouts to be compared under the same knowledge state. The resulting step-level advantages are then fused with trajectory-level advantages to produce token-level training signals. In this way, EG-GRPO provides task-grounded supervision for intermediate evidence acquisition while retaining the final outcome signal, enabling more precise credit assignment for deep search agents. We systematically evaluate EG-GRPO on five deep search benchmarks: BrowseComp ( Wei et al., 2025 ) , BrowseComp-ZH ( Zhou et al., 2025 ) , GAIA ( Mialon et al., 2023 ) , xBenchDS-2505 and xBenchDS-2510 ( Chen et al., 2025 ) . EG-GRPO consistently outperforms the GRPO baseline as well as reward-enhanced and step-level baselines, demonstrating that step-level credit assignment provides a complementary training signal to trajectory-level rewards. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: • Through step-level analysis of rollout trajectories, we reveal a strong correlation between the quality of incremental evidence acquisition and final answer correctness, with the most pronounced divergence emerging early in the search process. This provides empirical evidence for the need for step-level credit assignment in deep search RL. • We propose EG-GRPO , which transforms task-grounded evidence claims from synthetic training data into dense step-level rewards and employs hierarchical fallback normalization for stable advantage estimation, without requiring additional human annotations or auxiliary model training. • We conduct extensive experiments across five deep search benchmarks, demonstrating the effectiveness of EG-GRPO. Comprehensive ablation studies further validate the contribution of its key components.

sections.heading: Synthetic Multi-Hop Data Generation.
sections.text: Modern deep search datasets ( Lu et al., 2025 ; Du et al., 2026 ; Chu et al., 2026 ) leverage entity-centric knowledge graph traversal and information obfuscation to automatically construct complex multi-hop questions. During data generation, a structured sequence of factual relations is used to connect a seed entity to the target answer, yielding a set of intermediate factual claims required to resolve the query.

The step-level advantage is then computed by normalizing its discounted return within the selected group: A i , t S = G i , t − mean ⁡ ( { G j , u : ( j , u ) ∈ 𝒢 i , t } ) std ⁡ ( { G j , u : ( j , u ) ∈ 𝒢 i , t } ) . (13) If the exact-state group contains insufficient samples, we fall back to the state-size group; if that group is also insufficient, we use the query-global group. The final level requires only two samples within the query group, ensuring that a normalization baseline is available for valid rollouts. The hierarchy provides a trade-off between precision and statistical robustness. Level 1 compares steps taken from identical knowledge states and therefore provides the most fine-grained credit signal. However, exact states can be sparse because different rollouts often acquire evidence in different orders. Level 2 relaxes the criterion to states containing the same number of known claims, preserving a coarse notion of comparability while increasing the number of matched samples. Level 3 further falls back to all steps associated with the same query, ensuring broad coverage when finer-grained matches are unavailable. After normalization, the step-level advantage is clipped to [ − C , C ] [-C,C] . The resulting scalar is broadcast to all decision-related tokens within the corresponding turn segment, providing a dense and forward-looking supervisory signal for policy optimization.

sections.heading: Tool server.
sections.text: The agent engages with the live web through two tools: the search tool, which queries the Serper API ( ser, 2025 ) and retrieves top‑10 snippets along with their associated URLs, and the visit tool, which extracts page content from a given URL via the Jina API ( jin, 2025 ) .

sections.heading: Baselines.
sections.text: We compare EG-GRPO with the following RL algorithms: (1) GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) , which uses a binary outcome reward (0/1 score). (2) C-GRPO ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , which combines a rubric-based citation score and outcome reward for training robust deep search agents. (3) GiGPO ( Feng et al., 2025 ) , which uses fine-grained credit assignment for LLM agents while preserving the appealing properties of group-based RL. (4) STAMP ( Xu et al., 2026 ) , which leverages provenance-guided supervision to perform fine-grained step-level credit assignment across search trajectories. We also provide the reported scores of several state‑of‑the‑art search agents for reference (see Appendix B for details).

sections.heading: Training Details.
sections.text: We evaluate EG-GRPO across two base model architectures: Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 (dense) and Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507 (MoE) ( Yang et al., 2025 ) . The training pipeline consists of a cold-start Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) stage using 1,000 high-quality trajectories selected from OpenSeeker ( Du et al., 2026 ) , followed by RL training on 2,316 synthesized prompts. We employ Qwen-Flash ( Yang et al., 2025 ) as the judge LLM for both final-answer reward scoring and step-level evidence verification. Full hyperparameters, training parameters, and hardware configurations are detailed in Appendix D .

sections.heading: Benchmarks and Evaluation Details.
sections.text: The evaluation of our trained agents is conducted on five challenging deep search benchmarks: BrowseComp ( Wei et al., 2025 ) , BrowseComp‑ZH ( Zhou et al., 2025 ) , the text‑only validation subset of GAIA ( Mialon et al., 2023 ) , xBenchDS-2505 and xBenchDS-2510 ( Chen et al., 2025 ) . We use Qwen-Flash ( Yang et al., 2025 ) as judge LLM to determine if the agent’s final response agrees with the ground truth. We evaluate each model at 128k context length.

sections.heading: 4.2 Main Results
sections.text: (a) Outcome Reward (b) Average Tool Call Steps (c) Average Evidence Coverage Figure 3: Training dynamics of GRPO and EG-GRPO on 4B models, including the changes of outcome rewards, average tool call steps and evidence coverage. Table 2 summarizes the overall performance of EG-GRPO and various baselines across five challenging deep search benchmarks. Across both 4B and 30B model architectures, EG-GRPO generally outperforms the standard GRPO baseline as well as fine-grained reward-enhanced methods, achieving average accuracy gains of 4.96 and 3.64 over GRPO, respectively. Notably, GiGPO underperforms standard GRPO on both xBench-DS-2505 and xBench-DS-2510, suggesting that generic state-based grouping may be less effective for some long-horizon search tasks. In contrast, EG-GRPO demonstrates robust and consistent improvements; for instance, on the Qwen3-4B, it improves over standard GRPO by 11.11 absolute points on GAIA (45.9 vs. 34.8). These results demonstrate that task-grounded evidence supervision provides an effective complementary signal to trajectory-level outcome rewards for deep search RL.

sections.heading: Training Dynamics.
sections.text: Figure 3(a) demonstrates that both GRPO and EG-GRPO successfully optimize the outcome reward during training, with EG-GRPO exhibiting comparable or slightly better performance in later epochs. Concurrently, Figure 3(b) reveals a distinct difference in the agents’ search behaviors. While the baseline GRPO shows a sharp decline in average tool calls, suggesting a tendency to terminate searches prematurely, EG-GRPO maintains a more gradual reduction. This indicates that step-level supervision helps mitigate the risk of the agent taking superficial shortcuts, encouraging sufficient interaction with the environment before formulating an answer.

sections.heading: Evidence Acquisition.
sections.text: The impact of this sustained exploration is reflected in the agents’ evidence acquisition capabilities, as depicted in Figure 3(c) . While the standard GRPO model struggles to consistently increase its evidence coverage throughout training, EG-GRPO demonstrates a steady upward trend. This observation suggests that the evidence-guided step-level signals effectively guide the agent to progressively uncover the necessary factual evidence, rather than merely optimizing for the sparse outcome reward.

sections.heading: Effect of Fallback Grouping Strategy.
sections.text: We evaluate the three-level fallback normalization by comparing the full strategy with two boundary cases: Level 1 only (exact-state grouping) and Level 3 only (prompt-global normalization). As shown in Table 4 , the full strategy achieves the best overall performance across the five benchmarks, although prompt-global normalization slightly outperforms it on GAIA. Exact-state grouping suffers from sparse matches among divergent rollouts, while global normalization ignores differences in intermediate knowledge states and introduces noisier comparisons. sections.heading: Reinforcement Learning for Deep Search Agents.
sections.text: Reinforcement learning has become an effective paradigm for training deep search agents to perform long-horizon information retrieval and reasoning. Early approaches such as Search-R1 ( Jin et al., 2025 ) and DeepDive ( Lu et al., 2025 ) employ outcome-based rewards on automatically constructed multi-hop search tasks, while subsequent systems further scale this paradigm through synthetic data generation and large-scale RL ( Gao et al., 2025 ; Du et al., 2026 ; Chu et al., 2026 ) . However, binary outcome rewards provide limited supervision for long search trajectories. Recent work therefore exploits auxiliary annotations from synthetic data to construct richer trajectory-level rewards. E-GRPO ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) leverages ground-truth entity information to derive dense entity-aware rewards, while CaRR ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) decomposes complex questions into verifiable single-hop rubrics and incorporates citation correctness into the reward. These approaches provide more informative supervision, but their rewards remain scalar signals assigned at the trajectory level.

sections.heading: Step-Level Credit Assignment.
sections.text: Process Reward Models (PRMs) provide intermediate-step supervision for mathematical reasoning ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) , while GiGPO ( Feng et al., 2025 ) introduces state-based grouping to estimate step-level relative advantages for long-horizon LLM agents. More recently, STAMP ( Xu et al., 2026 ) further assigns step-level credit through provenance tracing, identifying the first retrieval action that exposes supporting evidence. In contrast, EG-GRPO uses task-grounded evidence claims annotated in synthetic training data as the supervision units, rewarding newly acquired claims and representing their cumulative set as an explicit knowledge state for state-conditioned advantage estimation. This provides evidence-grounded process supervision without additional human process annotations or auxiliary reward-model training.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: In this paper, we introduced EG-GRPO, a novel reinforcement learning framework that addresses the challenge of sparse rewards in training deep search agents by enabling step-level credit assignment. By leveraging task-grounded evidence claims available in synthetic training data, our method derives dense, task-grounded process rewards without requiring additional human process annotations. To ensure robust and fair advantage estimation, EG-GRPO aligns intermediate actions based on cumulative knowledge states and applies a hierarchical fallback normalization strategy. Extensive evaluations across multiple deep search benchmarks demonstrate that EG-GRPO consistently improves over standard trajectory-level RL and achieves strong performance against existing fine-grained baselines across different model scales. Ultimately, this step-level supervision effectively guides agents to sustain multi-turn exploration and systematically acquire the evidence needed to solve complex search tasks, paving the way for more capable and reliable long-horizon search models.

sections.heading: AI Use Statement
sections.text: In this work, we used generative AI tools for LLM-based judging and annotation within the research pipeline, including final-answer correctness scoring, step-level evidence verification, evidence-claim matching, identification of the first supporting citation for each claim, and automated construction of synthetic evidence claims. Additionally, we used generative AI tools for code development assistance and language editing during manuscript preparation. We reviewed all AI-assisted work, manually verified the reliability of the LLM judge on sampled trajectories, and checked all generated data, annotations, judge outputs, code, and manuscript text. The authors designed the research and experiments, validated and quality-controlled the generated data and annotations, verified implementation correctness and experimental results, and interpreted the findings, and we take full responsibility for the final content of this work.

sections.heading: Reproducibility Statement
sections.text: We provide sufficient detail to reproduce the proposed EG-GRPO training and evaluation pipeline. Section 3 specifies evidence-claim construction, evidence-to-trajectory attribution, incremental step rewards, cumulative knowledge states, three-level fallback grouping, and the final training objective. Section 4 describes the tool server, baselines, benchmarks, model scales, cold-start SFT and RL training setup, evaluation protocol, main results, analyses, and ablation studies. Appendix D reports the full SFT and RL configurations, including model initialization, optimization hyperparameters, hardware, batch sizes, context lengths, and EG-GRPO hyperparameters ( w = 0.5 w=0.5 , γ = 0.95 \gamma=0.95 , C = 5 C=5 ). We provide anonymized implementation code and scripts for reproducing the main experiments in the supplementary material.

sections.heading: C.1 Synthetic QA Construction
sections.text: We construct synthetic deep-search queries from structured factual paths derived from an entity-centric knowledge source. Starting from a seed entity, we traverse a multi-hop factual path to obtain a sequence of related entities and factual relations. The resulting path is then transformed into a natural-language question through entity obfuscation, where intermediate entities that should be recovered through search are replaced by descriptive clues while preserving the underlying factual dependencies. This construction process produces questions that require the agent to progressively recover hidden information through multi-step web search rather than directly matching an entity mentioned in the query. The path length and the number of hidden entities are used to control the reasoning complexity of the synthesized questions.

sections.heading: C.2 Evidence Claim Extraction
sections.text: The structured factual paths used for question synthesis are further converted into atomic evidence claims. For each synthesized query q q , we obtain a set 𝒞 q = { c 1 , … , c K } , \mathcal{C}_{q}=\{c_{1},\ldots,c_{K}\}, where each c k c_{k} is a self-contained factual assertion that can be independently verified from web evidence. Claims are normalized to a consistent granularity so that each claim represents a single verifiable fact required for resolving the query. For example, for the query: A European tour that concluded in a year when a film about a U.S. president was released, and which visited a continent where a writer published research on African literature containing the word ’polyphony’ - what was the academic journal where that research appeared? The original structured facts can be converted into claims such as: • c 1 c_{1} : The Carpe Diem Tour concluded in 2012. • c 2 c_{2} : The film Lincoln was released in 2012. • c 3 c_{3} : The Carpe Diem Tour visited Europe. • c 4 c_{4} : The Carpe Diem Tour visited Africa. • c 5 c_{5} : Ken Walibora’s research was related to Africa. • c 6 c_{6} : Ken Walibora published research in Research in African Literatures . • c 7 c_{7} : The relevant research article contains “polyphony” in its title. These claims constitute the task-grounded evidence units used by EG-GRPO. Although the claims originate from the structured synthesis process, their internal dependency relations are not used by the training algorithm.

sections.heading: C.3 Claim Verification and Filtering
sections.text: To ensure that the extracted evidence claims provide reliable supervision, we apply automatic verification and filtering to the synthesized data. Each claim is required to satisfy three criteria: (1) it represents a concrete factual assertion rather than a vague description; (2) it is independently verifiable from publicly available web evidence; and (3) it provides information that is relevant to resolving the corresponding query. We further remove samples containing redundant, ambiguous, or unverifiable claims. Claims that require substantial inference beyond the retrieved evidence are also excluded. The resulting claim set is used as the task-grounded evidence annotation for subsequent RL training.

sections.heading: SFT.
sections.text: We filtered 1,000 high-quality SFT trajectories from the OpenSeeker ( Du et al., 2026 ) dataset and adapted them to match the trajectory format used in this paper. Using this dataset, we fine-tuned both the 4B and 30B models for 1 epoch. The training was conducted on 8 × \times NVIDIA H800 GPUs with a batch size of 32, a learning rate of 2 × 10 − 5 2\times 10^{-5} , and a maximum context length of 128k.

sections.heading: RL.
sections.text: Starting from the SFT checkpoints, we conducted RL training on 2,316 synthetic data across 16 × \times NVIDIA H800 GPUs for 2 epochs, based on verl framework ( Jiang et al., 2025 ) . The training used a learning rate of 1 × 10 − 6 1\times 10^{-6} and a maximum context length of 64k. For experience collection, we set the prompt batch size to 32 and sampled 8 completions per prompt, yielding a global batch size of 256. Generation parameters during rollout were set to a temperature of 1.0, top_p = 0.95 \text{top\_p}=0.95 , top_k = 20 \text{top\_k}=20 , and a presence penalty of 1.1. For the EG-GRPO advantage calculation, we set the step-level advantage weight w = 0.5 w=0.5 , discount factor γ = 0.95 \gamma=0.95 , and clipping threshold C = 5 C=5 . We employed Qwen-Flash ( Yang et al., 2025 ) as the judge LLM to perform both final-answer reward scoring and step-level evidence verification.

sections.heading: Appendix E Human Verification of LLM Judge
sections.text: To assess the reliability of the LLM judge in identifying evidence acquisition within the EG-GRPO framework, we conducted a manual review of its judgments across 10 randomly sampled deep search trajectories. The sampled trajectories cover 67 evidence claims. Using human assessments as the gold standard, annotators independently verified whether each evidence claim was sufficiently supported by the retrieved information and, when supported, identified the first citation that provided sufficient evidence. We then compared the human annotations with the corresponding LLM judge outputs. The LLM judge achieves 91.0% accuracy in identifying whether evidence claims are supported and 94.0% accuracy in identifying the first supporting citation. These results indicate that the LLM judge can reliably identify evidence acquisition and its corresponding supporting citations in search trajectories.

Affiliation: Renmin University of China, Beijing 100872, China Affiliation: Key Laboratory of Data Engineering and Knowledge Engineering, MOE, China Email: zhang-jing@ruc.edu.cn Abstract LLM-based search agents demonstrate strong capabilities in long-horizon information seeking and reasoning, typically trained via reinforcement learning. However, existing approaches predominantly rely on trajectory-level outcome rewards, providing limited supervision for complex search and reasoning processes. Although step-level credit assignment offers a promising solution, obtaining reliable and task-grounded supervision for open-ended search remains challenging. In this paper, we propose E vidence- G uided G roup R elative P olicy O ptimization ( EG-GRPO ), a framework that derives step-level supervision from the evidence annotations available in synthetic deep search data. EG-GRPO identifies the first supporting citation for each required evidence claim and uses the newly acquired evidence to construct step-level process rewards. By representing the accumulated evidence as an evolving knowledge state, EG-GRPO further performs state-conditioned relative advantage estimation and combines the resulting step-level signal with the standard trajectory-level outcome advantage. Experiments on five challenging deep search benchmarks show that EG-GRPO generally outperforms standard GRPO and existing reward-enhanced and step-level RL baselines across different model scales. These results demonstrate that task-grounded evidence annotations can provide effective process supervision for credit assignment in deep search RL. 1 Introduction As the capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance, deep search agents have demonstrated immense potential in tackling knowledge-intensive tasks ( OpenAI, 2025 ; Xi et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2024 ) . Grounded in the ReAct paradigm, these agents iteratively gather evidence within noisy web environments by alternating between reasoning, tool utilization, and observation, ultimately providing well-supported answers ( Yao et al., 2023 ) . To further enhance their long-horizon information retrieval capabilities, Reinforcement Learning (RL) has emerged as the prevalent paradigm for training deep search agents. Existing work typically uses a binary outcome reward as the training signal on synthetic multi‑hop QA datasets, comparing the agent’s final answer against the ground truth ( Jin et al., 2025 ; Gao et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025b ) . In deep search scenarios, a complete trajectory typically comprises anywhere from several to over a dozen retrieval iterations, with each retrieval action potentially exerting a critical impact on the final answer formulation. However, the entire trajectory receives only a single binary scalar signal at its conclusion, leaving the model unable to discern which specific retrieval step played the decisive role ( Shao et al., 2025 ) . To alleviate this reward sparsity issue, several studies have attempted to introduce richer reward signals at the trajectory level ( Gunjal et al., 2026 ; Lu et al., 2025 ) . E-GRPO ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) leverages entity annotations in synthetic data to formulate an entity matching rate as a fine-grained reward; CaRR ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) further decomposes questions into single-hop rubrics, combining context-aware rubric rewards and outcome rewards in RL. Although these methods yield substantial improvements in their respective evaluation settings, they fundamentally still calculate a scalar reward for the entire trajectory. Consequently, the core issue of differentiated step-level credit assignment remains unresolved. Step-level credit assignment provides a more direct approach to alleviating the aforementioned problem and has been extensively studied in sequential reasoning ( Zhang, 2026 ; Guo et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . Process Reward Models (PRMs) provide step-level supervision over intermediate reasoning steps, offering a more direct training signal than outcome-only rewards ( Lightman et al., 2024 ; Pala et al., 2025 ) . Meanwhile, GiGPO ( Feng et al., 2025 ) introduces state-based grouping to estimate step-level relative advantages for long-horizon LLM agents. Recently, STAMP ( Xu et al., 2026 ) further extends step-level credit assignment to deep search agents by tracing evidence provenance and attributing credit to the first retrieval action that exposes supporting evidence. However, applying such approaches to open-ended deep search still faces two key challenges. First, search actions lack a well-defined notion of local correctness: a retrieval step may be valuable for discovering direct evidence, uncovering indirect clues, or narrowing the search space, making reliable and task-grounded step-level supervision difficult to obtain. Second, fine-grained credit assignment requires a meaningful representation of the evolving search state, whereas raw multi-turn search histories are highly heterogeneous and difficult to match reliably. These challenges motivate us to look beyond external process supervision and ask whether a task-grounded step-level signal is already available in the synthetic data used to train deep search agents. We observe that such supervisory signals are inherently embedded in synthetic data pipelines. Current deep search datasets are often constructed through knowledge‑graph random walks and information obfuscation, which produce structured annotations describing the factual evidence needed to answer each query ( Lu et al., 2025 ; Du et al., 2026 ) . Traditionally, only question‑answer pairs are retained for reward computation, discarding this rich annotation. However, the annotated evidence claims provide a natural source of task-grounded step-level supervision, as they specify the factual information that a successful trajectory should progressively acquire. To test this hypothesis, we conducted an experiment on a subset of the training set (320 prompts) by sampling 8 trajectories per prompt and computing the evidence coverage rate for each trajectory. Figure 1 (left) shows that correct trajectories have significantly higher coverage (median 41.97% vs. 26.29%), confirming coverage as a strong predictor of final correctness. Figure 1 (right) further reveals that correct trajectories maintain higher cumulative coverage from the very beginning, and this gap widens as retrieval proceeds. These observations indicate that evidence acquisition is a continuous process signal highly correlated with task success. More importantly, the cumulative set of acquired evidence claims provides an explicit representation of the agent’s evolving knowledge state, allowing rollouts to be compared under identical evidence states without manual process annotation. This observation motivates us to use task-grounded evidence annotations as a source of step-level supervision for deep search RL. Building upon these insights, we propose E vidence- G uided G roup R elative P olicy O ptimization ( EG-GRPO ), a step-level credit assignment method for deep search agents. EG-GRPO transforms the evidence claims annotated in synthetic data into dense process rewards and combines them with GRPO’s trajectory-level advantages, preserving outcome supervision while providing fine-grained guidance for intermediate retrieval actions. Specifically, an LLM-based judge identifies the first supporting citation for each required evidence claim, and newly supported claims at each step are converted into process rewards. We further define a cumulative knowledge state based on the evidence claims acquired before each step and perform state-conditioned advantage normalization, enabling different rollouts to be compared under the same knowledge state. The resulting step-level advantages are then fused with trajectory-level advantages to produce token-level training signals. In this way, EG-GRPO provides task-grounded supervision for intermediate evidence acquisition while retaining the final outcome signal, enabling more precise credit assignment for deep search agents. We systematically evaluate EG-GRPO on five deep search benchmarks: BrowseComp ( Wei et al., 2025 ) , BrowseComp-ZH ( Zhou et al., 2025 ) , GAIA ( Mialon et al., 2023 ) , xBenchDS-2505 and xBenchDS-2510 ( Chen et al., 2025 ) . EG-GRPO consistently outperforms the GRPO baseline as well as reward-enhanced and step-level baselines, demonstrating that step-level credit assignment provides a complementary training signal to trajectory-level rewards. Reinforcement learning has become an effective paradigm for training deep search agents to perform long-horizon information retrieval and reasoning. Early approaches such as Search-R1 ( Jin et al., 2025 ) and DeepDive ( Lu et al., 2025 ) employ outcome-based rewards on automatically constructed multi-hop search tasks, while subsequent systems further scale this paradigm through synthetic data generation and large-scale RL ( Gao et al., 2025 ; Du et al., 2026 ; Chu et al., 2026 ) . However, binary outcome rewards provide limited supervision for long search trajectories. Recent work therefore exploits auxiliary annotations from synthetic data to construct richer trajectory-level rewards. E-GRPO ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) leverages ground-truth entity information to derive dense entity-aware rewards, while CaRR ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) decomposes complex questions into verifiable single-hop rubrics and incorporates citation correctness into the reward. These approaches provide more informative supervision, but their rewards remain scalar signals assigned at the trajectory level. Step-Level Credit Assignment. Process Reward Models (PRMs) provide intermediate-step supervision for mathematical reasoning ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) , while GiGPO ( Feng et al., 2025 ) introduces state-based grouping to estimate step-level relative advantages for long-horizon LLM agents. More recently, STAMP ( Xu et al., 2026 ) further assigns step-level credit through provenance tracing, identifying the first retrieval action that exposes supporting evidence. In contrast, EG-GRPO uses task-grounded evidence claims annotated in synthetic training data as the supervision units, rewarding newly acquired claims and representing their cumulative set as an explicit knowledge state for state-conditioned advantage estimation. This provides evidence-grounded process supervision without additional human process annotations or auxiliary reward-model training. 6 Conclusion In this paper, we introduced EG-GRPO, a novel reinforcement learning framework that addresses the challenge of sparse rewards in training deep search agents by enabling step-level credit assignment. By leveraging task-grounded evidence claims available in synthetic training data, our method derives dense, task-grounded process rewards without requiring additional human process annotations. To ensure robust and fair advantage estimation, EG-GRPO aligns intermediate actions based on cumulative knowledge states and applies a hierarchical fallback normalization strategy. Extensive evaluations across multiple deep search benchmarks demonstrate that EG-GRPO consistently improves over standard trajectory-level RL and achieves strong performance against existing fine-grained baselines across different model scales. Ultimately, this step-level supervision effectively guides agents to sustain multi-turn exploration and systematically acquire the evidence needed to solve complex search tasks, paving the way for more capable and reliable long-horizon search models. Appendix C Data Synthesis Details C.1 Synthetic QA Construction We construct synthetic deep-search queries from structured factual paths derived from an entity-centric knowledge source. Starting from a seed entity, we traverse a multi-hop factual path to obtain a sequence of related entities and factual relations. The resulting path is then transformed into a natural-language question through entity obfuscation, where intermediate entities that should be recovered through search are replaced by descriptive clues while preserving the underlying factual dependencies. This construction process produces questions that require the agent to progressively recover hidden information through multi-step web search rather than directly matching an entity mentioned in the query. The path length and the number of hidden entities are used to control the reasoning complexity of the synthesized questions. C.2 Evidence Claim Extraction The structured factual paths used for question synthesis are further converted into atomic evidence claims. For each synthesized query q q , we obtain a set 𝒞 q = { c 1 , … , c K } , \mathcal{C}_{q}=\{c_{1},\ldots,c_{K}\}, where each c k c_{k} is a self-contained factual assertion that can be independently verified from web evidence. Claims are normalized to a consistent granularity so that each claim represents a single verifiable fact required for resolving the query. For example, for the query: A European tour that concluded in a year when a film about a U.S. president was released, and which visited a continent where a writer published research on African literature containing the word ’polyphony’ - what was the academic journal where that research appeared? The original structured facts can be converted into claims such as: • c 1 c_{1} : The Carpe Diem Tour concluded in 2012. • c 2 c_{2} : The film Lincoln was released in 2012. • c 3 c_{3} : The Carpe Diem Tour visited Europe. • c 4 c_{4} : The Carpe Diem Tour visited Africa. • c 5 c_{5} : Ken Walibora’s research was related to Africa. • c 6 c_{6} : Ken Walibora published research in Research in African Literatures . • c 7 c_{7} : The relevant research article contains “polyphony” in its title. These claims constitute the task-grounded evidence units used by EG-GRPO. Although the claims originate from the structured synthesis process, their internal dependency relations are not used by the training algorithm. C.3 Claim Verification and Filtering To ensure that the extracted evidence claims provide reliable supervision, we apply automatic verification and filtering to the synthesized data. Each claim is required to satisfy three criteria: (1) it represents a concrete factual assertion rather than a vague description; (2) it is independently verifiable from publicly available web evidence; and (3) it provides information that is relevant to resolving the corresponding query. We further remove samples containing redundant, ambiguous, or unverifiable claims. Claims that require substantial inference beyond the retrieved evidence are also excluded. The resulting claim set is used as the task-grounded evidence annotation for subsequent RL training. Appendix D Training Configuration SFT. We filtered 1,000 high-quality SFT trajectories from the OpenSeeker ( Du et al., 2026 ) dataset and adapted them to match the trajectory format used in this paper. Using this dataset, we fine-tuned both the 4B and 30B models for 1 epoch. The training was conducted on 8 × \times NVIDIA H800 GPUs with a batch size of 32, a learning rate of 2 × 10 − 5 2\times 10^{-5} , and a maximum context length of 128k. RL. Starting from the SFT checkpoints, we conducted RL training on 2,316 synthetic data across 16 × \times NVIDIA H800 GPUs for 2 epochs, based on verl framework ( Jiang et al., 2025 ) . The training used a learning rate of 1 × 10 − 6 1\times 10^{-6} and a maximum context length of 64k. For experience collection, we set the prompt batch size to 32 and sampled 8 completions per prompt, yielding a global batch size of 256. Generation parameters during rollout were set to a temperature of 1.0, top_p = 0.95 \text{top\_p}=0.95 , top_k = 20 \text{top\_k}=20 , and a presence penalty of 1.1. For the EG-GRPO advantage calculation, we set the step-level advantage weight w = 0.5 w=0.5 , discount factor γ = 0.95 \gamma=0.95 , and clipping threshold C = 5 C=5 . We employed Qwen-Flash ( Yang et al., 2025 ) as the judge LLM to perform both final-answer reward scoring and step-level evidence verification. Appendix E Human Verification of LLM Judge To assess the reliability of the LLM judge in identifying evidence acquisition within the EG-GRPO framework, we conducted a manual review of its judgments across 10 randomly sampled deep search trajectories. The sampled trajectories cover 67 evidence claims. Using human assessments as the gold standard, annotators independently verified whether each evidence claim was sufficiently supported by the retrieved information and, when supported, identified the first citation that provided sufficient evidence. We then compared the human annotations with the corresponding LLM judge outputs. The LLM judge achieves 91.0% accuracy in identifying whether evidence claims are supported and 94.0% accuracy in identifying the first supporting citation. These results indicate that the LLM judge can reliably identify evidence acquisition and its corresponding supporting citations in search trajectories.
